subsubtopic: LACK OF SUMMER JOBS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr, Speaker, in view of the fact that, on the one hand, thousands of young people will be unemployed this summer and that, on the other hand, there is a shortage of skilled manpower in the farming industry, I request the unanimous consent of the House pursuant to Standing Order 43 in order to move a motion concerning this very important and extremely urgent matter. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise):
That a special committee of this House be created without any further delay in order to consider the serious problem of youth unemployment, as well as the shortage of skilled agricultural manpower, and that the said committee be instructed to make recommendations to the minister in order to solve this problem and to report to this House before June 15, 1973.

subtopic: CAR RENTAL CONCESSIONS AT MINISTRY AIRPORTS

1. The
policy of the Ministry of Transport with respect to car rental concessions is: (a) The company must be able to serve at least 50 per cent of the Ministry's Airports which already have car rental service and the system must be established in the cities served by those airports; (b) The company must have a Canadian head office with which the Ministry would negotiate, and which would be signatory to the agreement with the Ministry i.e., the Ministry would not deal with individual franchised operators; (c) If the company meets these two criteria it would be required to pay an annual guaranteed fee equal to the average annual concession fee being paid by the other car rental systems established at Ministry Airports.

6.	The limousine operations are licensed and controlled by provincial authorities. Concessions for the book and barber shops are not exclusive and are awarded on the basis of a public tender call. speechtext:

2.	Under the provisions of the Indian Act a Band Council may acquire parcels of reserve land from an individual Band member who has been placed in lawful possession of the land. An Acquisition of such land would include a house or any such improvements made to the property in question. The Indian Act stipulates, however, that Band held reserve land must be surrendered to the Crown before it can be leased to non-Indians. The leases are entered into with the Crown and moneys collected are credited to the account of the Band concerned.
3.	A certificate of Possession is the documentary evidence of an Indian's right to lawful possession of the reserve land described therein and entitles him to quiet possession of the land. A Certificate of Occupation is evidence of an Indian's right to temporary possession of the reserve lands described therein and is normally issued subject to the fulfillment of certain conditions as to the use and settlement of the land. The Certificate of Occupation is issued for a term of two years and may be extended for a further two year period. It is replaced by a Certificate of Possession upon fulfillment of the necessary conditions.

In the case of those honours which are in the prerogative of the Crown, the government of Canada is informed by the Crown but the government of Canada does not exercise a veto.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not every day that one has such an audience in the Commons, and I want to thank all hon. members for their willingness to listen to my remarks. As a mark of appreciation, I might point out that while I have 20 minutes ahead of me I intend to use only about five.
In a somewhat more serious vein, I want to conclude what I said the other day on the question of capital punishment with a reference to one of the aspects of capital punishment which has troubled me the most. I refer to the question of responsibility when it comes to murder, and the matter of justice in the administration of capital punishment. I want to illustrate my concern or the sort of thing that arouses my concern with a story.
One day a woman who was a grandmother called me and asked me to help her grandson. She said: "The boy is 12 years old and he is going to kill somebody. There is something wrong with the boy. He has been abandoned by his father, his mother is working and trying to help out, but the boy has some serious difficulty and I need some help". I spent the better part of the day calling provincial agencies to find out whether I could get some assistance for this woman. I was told by one that they had room for seven disturbed boys in various institutions in that area, that his was the eighth so there was no place for him. They were very sympathetic and understood the problem, but this was one of the difficulties.
I thought to myself that when this boy grows up, and if the fears of this woman are realized, who will be responsible in that case; will it be the boy who becomes a murderer, will it be the mother or will it be society? When that 12 year old boy needed help he could not find it, so surely society has to bear some share of the blame. This is

May 16, 1973
Capital Punishment
the great dilemma. When you read the biography of some of the assassins of United States political figures, one story emerges. One assassin was a seriously disturbed child. The authorities went to the mother and told her that the boy needed psychiatric care. The mother refused to believe them, feeling this could not be true of her son. When the child grew up, he became a murderer. Who was guilty in that particular case; was it the boy, the mother or society? In virtually every case I have been able to trace in respect of a murderer, I have found a history of a sordid childhood or a history of violence of one kind or another. People do not suddenly become murderers as adults.
If we are really serious, and I have no reason to believe that this House is anything else, about protecting society, and in many ways this is what the debate is all about, then we should stop thinking in terms of hanging murderers. We should stop kidding ourselves that this is the way to protect society. This may be the easy and facile way. It may be reassuring to say that a man is guilty, we will put him out of the way and that is the end of it. That is not the end of it because you cannot bring back a life in that way, nor can you prevent a future crime by that means. If we are serious about this matter of protecting society, we must deal with it at another level. We must know more about the causes of murder. We must remove some of the environmental circumstances that create an atmosphere in which this takes place, and we must concentrate much more on providing assistance to young people who are disturbed in order to make sure that society is adequately protected in the future.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject which involves us today is as basic as any that this or any parliament will ever face. It involves life and death, the safety of the individual and the orderliness of our society. These are not issues with which the House can deal summarily, and it did not do so in 1967. Nor are they issues which individuals can resolve easily within their consciences. We are called upon to exercise wisdom and judgment and calmness of decision in respect of a subject which summons emotion and evokes often our most basic passions.
That we cannot all agree on this issue is understandable, for we are dealing with justice which is always a fleeting concept, and almost always subjective. George Eliot wrote:
Who shall put his finger on the work of justice, and say "It is there?" Justice is like the Kingdom of God-it is not without us as a fact, it is within us as a great yearning.
I am reminded also of the French poet, Paul Claudel who said:

Justice is masked, not blindfolded and no-one knows who it is. [English]
If Canada be a civilized place, it is that way because of the concern which Canadians have for one another. Canadians take an interest in one another, look out for one another, help one another. We have managed to avoid here many of the hatreds which are troublesome elsewhere. We have retained in Canada the compassion for our neighbour

which in some places has been replaced by indifference, and in others by fear.
This has permitted us to accept many propositions in Canada which are often still argued about elsewhere. We accept the proposition, for instance, that no one should suffer from lack of medical treatment or, treated, suffer from the financial burden of that treatment. We accept the proposition that the aged, having contributed to our society, should be given the opportunity to live with as much dignity and grace as our resources will permit. We accept the proposition that every child should be educated equally, and that the gifted be given the opportunity to fulfil their promise. We accept the proposition that the needy and the handicapped should be assisted by those able to do so.
We also accept the proposition, from which many of my remarks during today's debate will follow, that the wayward should be helped to return to a life that is useful and wholesome. We accept these propositions and willingly bear their cost because we believe they contribute to a better society: One that is open, not authoritative; one that is creative, not stultifying, and one that is understanding, not spiteful.

Underlying all of these characteristics, which make our society so human, is the belief by Canadians that in such a social system they can flourish and pursue their lives free from fear of lawless elements. But without confidence in lawful processes, and in the law enforcement agencies, no community is willing to extend a helping hand to those who have broken the law. The most understanding of persons, in the face of lawless activity, will harden his attitude and will refuse to accommodate changes. Out of fear for his safety, and for the safety of his loved ones, even the most merciful of men becomes unwilling to assist the wayward.
Accordingly, Mr. Speaker, in this debate of the issue of capital punishment, I suggest that the premise from which we must begin our discussion is the basic one of the safety of Canadians. Our criminal laws, our penal system, our reform programs will be of little value if they do not respect the right of Canadians to live their lives without fear of criminal activity. The attributes of mercy and forgiveness cannot thrive in circumstances of fright and uncertainty. In all our endeavours in this House to remove undue harshness from the criminal law, or to identify and alleviate the underlying social causes of crime, we must take care not to forfeit or endanger the safety of any law-abiding Canadian.
The Bail Reform law, the Parole Act, the various other criminal law amendments introduced in recent years, are all intended to relieve deserving persons from the indiscriminate application of severe sanctions in instances where these are found unnecessary. Those laws were not designed with any thought of trading off the safety of men, women and children in the pursuit of some social experiment. If those laws have been too loosely applied, as appears the case in certain instances, then it is the responsibility of the government to ensure through their administration that errors are not repeated. And as for us, at the federal government level this will be done wherever necessary.

So on the matter of capital punishment-I begin with two premises. The first is my belief that wanton or unnecessary killing is evil. The second is the requirement for self-protection, be it individual, or collective in the form of a society. Consequently, should killing be the only means to ensure survival against aggression-as in the case of self-defence of a human, or the self-defence of a society-then it is allowable. Life and freedom and justice are so valuable that they must be protected against an aggressor by whatever means are absolutely necessary in the circumstances, including the taking of life. The evidence available to us all has satisfied me beyond doubt that capital punishment-killing-is not effective as a deterrent against murder. Therefore, it is not justifiable for use by society as a means of self-defence.
In reality, the question before the House is what contribution to the safety of persons flows from retention or abolition of capital punishment. That is not a new question. It has been asked in the English legal system for hundreds of years. Pollack and Maitland tell us that under the Norman Kings "a wave of religious sentiment had set against capital punishment". And no wonder, for those learned authors recite the forms of punishment then in vogue: death inflicted by hanging, beheading, burning, drowning, stoning, precipitation from rocks; loss of ears, nose, upper lip, hands and feet; flogging and sale into slavery; emasculation and exoculation.
If the question of capital punishment has been asked for centuries, it has been answered in varying degrees for decades. The death penalty for such minor offences as pick-pocketing and petty theft was abandoned in England in the 19th century; in Canada it was abandoned for kidnapping and for rape in 1955. Public executions, once regarded as contributing to the deterrent effect, have not been practised in Canada since 1868. On each of those occasions, I have no doubt that questions were asked about the effectiveness of the penalty as a deterrent to that particular offence, and about the justness of the punishment having regard to the crime.
Capital punishment and abolition both have a long history in our social system and in its historic forebears. Much of what was once regarded as necessary and ordinary, now causes us all to shudder with revulsion at its cruelty and seeming disdain for human life. Yet it is not our function to judge in retrospect the morals or standards of bygone eras. It is for us to assess the necessity or lack of it, and the moral correctness or lack of it, of the death penalty for murder in Canada in 1973.
It is not my intention, Mr. Speaker, to discuss the statistical and other evidence bearing on this issue which is available to us all. I have weighed it carefully as I am sure have all hon. members. I have concluded to my own satisfaction that capital punishment is not an effective deterrent to murder.

On this point, because of the events of last weekend, I must digress slightly to cover the question of security of our penal institutions. Whatever the jail terms of convicted criminals, society must be able to assume that they will be enforced, and not broken willy-nilly by escape. Our prisons are there to contain unlawful persons. Containment is the primary function. Rehabilitation follows. I urge hon. members not to permit events of the past weekend to colour their views on the issue of capital punishment. Jailbreaks will be dealt with as the inquiries and the Solicitor General recommend. Amendments to other legislation will be viewed on their merits. But today, the issue is capital punishment, a punishment I do not regard to be effective for the only purpose advanced by its proponents, deterrence.

But there is such a thing as the royal prerogative of mercy, and it is one of the most civilized of the many prerogatives residing in the sovereign. As is the case with others, this particular prerogative is now exercised on Her Majesty's behalf in Canada by the Governor General in council. The royal prerogative of mercy is part of the law of Canada as, in some form or other, I believe it to be the part of the law of every country I know. Nor is the prerogative subject to the normal provisions of the Canadian criminal law, quite the contrary. The Criminal Code of Canada expressly states that nothing therein "in any manner limits or affects Her Majesty's royal prerogative of mercy".

Mr. Speaker, as has been said by many who have participated in this debate, the argument about capital punishment goes back a long way in human society and it involves an anxious moral question. I remind this House, if the members need reminding, that at the beginning, 100 or 200 years ago and longer than that, people were put to death for what we now consider minor offences, for theft of a loaf of bread, for example. I remind hon. members and the people of Canada that there has been a steady progress in civilized society away from that kind of treatment of offenders and that today in all modern western societies where the death penalty is retained, it is limited to a penalty for murder or for treason. I remind hon. members and the people of Canada that an increasing number of countries in the world have been abolishing the death penalty in their society.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that what has been happening over the decades is the progress of civilization in societies like our own. Progress in all directions; progress in the direction of social security; progress in the acceptance of the philosophic and social idea that we are indeed our brother's keepers; progress in the opposition to war unless it is unavoidable for the safety of society; progress in all directions of human behaviour, man to man and collectively, man to the creator. It is a major mark of the response which we have developed in a civilized society for human dignity and human life. I watched the abhorrence of the western world toward Naziism, Mr. Speaker, and I was impressed by the fact that it did not derive merely from an opposition to the social system that Hitlerism represented but it derived mainly from an aversion against the denigration of human dignity and the brutal destruction of human life for which Naziism was responsible.
I therefore make my first point, Mr. Speaker: historically, philosophically and morally, mankind in civilized society has been progressing away from the taking of human life by the state, by individual human beings and on a world scale. Continually and progressively, mankind

has recognized the dignity of the human being and the sacredness of the human life.
That takes me to the second point, Mr. Speaker, which it seems to me every hon. member must place before himself as he considers this question. The second point is that the state is justified in taking human life only if that taking of the human life protects society against a greater evil. This is the moral justification of some wars; it is the moral justification of military or police action against those who are in the act of threatening the security of the state or the lives of its citizens. The question we are asking ourselves during this debate, if we are serious as I am sure all of us are, is simply this: does the death penalty protect society against a greater evil so as to justify the state in taking a human life calculatedly and deliberately? I hope that every member of this House, I hope that every one of my fellow Canadians, that all of us are agreed that the state ought not deliberately to take a human life as an act of vengeance but that it would be justified only as an act of necessity to protect society.
The discussion here as elsewhere on this issue has been bedevilled by emotional reactions and by questioning motives. Mr. Speaker, there are some people who are in favour of the retention of capital punishment who accuse abolitionists of being bleeding hearts, more anxious to protect the criminal than to protect his victim. Some abolitionists accuse retentionists of being bloodless hearts lacking in moral concern. I hasten, before saying anything else, to admit that I well may have been guilty of this kind of attitude, as much as anyone else. Today, I suggest to hon. members adopting positions on both sides of this question that this is an unfortunate approach to the issue. We can discuss it constructively only if all of us assume that all of us and all Canadians are equally concerned about the moral and security problems involved and that those of us who are in favour of the abolition of capital punishment, as I am, are as concerned about the security of society and the state as any other person is, no matter, on which side of this argument he is. I believe that we would get much farther in understanding each other in this country and in arriving at a reasonable, legitimate and decent conclusion if we ceased accusing each other of motives on this anxious, moral question.

Next we come to the second argument for the retention of capital punishment, the deterrence argument. We have heard this argument time and again. We have heard the opposite argument time and again. I do not think anyone can say more; at least, I cannot. Having studied the subject for years, as have many other members of the House, because it is not only since becoming a Member of Parliament that I have been concerned about this, having been interested in it as a student, as a lawyer and all through my life, I think it is surely true to say that this at least is the case; There is no argument about the assertion that the statistical evidence does not support the allegation that capital punishment is a deterrent against murder. It may not support the opposite view. Logically speaking, there is no way in which you can support the opposite view.
There is no way in which you can find out how many people failed to commit murder because they thought that if they committed murder they might be executed. As I say, you cannot do that. The only statistical evidence you can have relates to the people who have already committed murder. Therefore, I do not claim that statistics show anything except that there is no correlation between the abolition or the retention of capital punishment and the number of violent crimes. All through history, according
Capital Punishment
to every statistical table I have ever seen, it has been shown that there has been, depending on the general social circumstances of a society, relatively the same rate of violent crime in jurisdictions that retained capital punishment as in jurisdictions that have abolished it. Over the years there has been no difference whatsoever between the rate of violent crime in jurisdictions that have retained capital punishment and jurisdictions that have not. So, I urge on all members this: all statistical evidence shows that there simply is no correlation between the two.
Indeed, some students of penology claim that it is more likely that, in the presence of capital punishment, more people who have committed the crime of homicide or murder are acquitted in court than is the case if there is not the threat of the death penalty. That makes sense to me. This is not merely the evidence arrived at as a result of surveys. Logic, as well, it seems to me supports that assertion. After all, juries in our society are composed of decent men and women and they are as anxious to avoid responsibility for the death of another human being as anyone in this House. That assertion seems logical to me and therefore I accept the result of the surveys and of the statistics, namely, that men and women on juries would hesitate a great deal more about finding someone guilty, if they knew that that finding would result in the death of the accused person, than would be the case if they knew that the accused would be in prison for life or would receive some sentence like that. Therefore I think there is good evidence from statistics and, it seems to me, logic for the proposition that more murderers are likely to get away by being acquitted in the presence of the threat of the death penalty under our kind of system, in which they would need to be convicted by a jury composed of men and women, than would be the case in a situation where the death penalty is not there.
Numerous studies have been made of murderers and people inclined to commit suicide. I am not a psychiatrist or a psychologist, but I am impressed by the fact that in all the reading I have done, in all the reports I have read on this subject, the experts are convinced that the murderer does not take into consideration the consequences of his act at the time of the murder. I do not know a single exception in the studies made by penologists, psychiatrists, psychologists and other experts in this field, though, of course, that may be my fault; exceptions may exist. Surely, this is the main consideration. Those who argue that the death sentence is a deterrent, accept by implication the proposition that a murderer is really a normal human being who says to himself along logical lines: If I commit murder I shall be hanged. He is not that kind of person, according to all the inquiries which have been made. He is not rational at the time of the act of murder, even though he might not, in legal terms, be considered insane as far as events at a trial are concerned.
Every study of which I am aware shows that the majority of murders, 60 or 70 per cent of them, or an even greater percentage than that, are committed among members of a family, among drinking companions, friends who have fallen out, men and women who are normally law-abiding citizens and who are driven by passion or some other uncontrollable emotion to kill someone else. I should like

May 16, 1973

to know how anyone thinks these people could be deterred by the threat of capital punishment. Many other murderers have been found through various studies to be psychotic, and I should like to know how they could be deterred by the threat of the death penalty. As far as the hardened criminal is concerned, the person who commits murder in the process of committing some other crime, every study shows he is invariably under the assumption that he will be able to get away with it. Otherwise, he would not have set out on the first crime.
Thus, I say to hon. members and to the people of Canada that the taking of life by the state by way of the death penalty accomplishes nothing as far as the protection of society is concerned, though it degrades the collectivity by having us murder someone else in response to a murder which has been committed. It is true there has been an increase recently in all crimes of violence, but I suggest that murder has not increased in any greater proportion than others and that the answer to an increase in violent crime does not lie in capital punishment or in other severe penalties. It lies in finding a way to overcome the increasing alienation in our society, it lies in improving the quality of life in a climate of growing urbanization, it lies in finding ways to eliminate poverty and deprivation, it lies in taking steps to improve the quality of life for all Canadians. It is in actions of this kind that the solution to violent crimes is to be found, not in violent penalties.

Like every other member of this House I am aware that a good many of my own constituents-I doubt from the replies to my questionnaire that it would be a majority-feel that the retention of capital punishment is necessary.
