subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with emotion that I rise today because we are living very serious, very difficult moments. What we are doing now will have great consequences on humanity and the life of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, we are told that this is a question of conscience, that every member is free to vote according to his conscience. But there are various kinds of consciences in this House, as I see it. Not many of them are alike. Not many of them really accept their responsibilities, which at times, are huge.

May 10, 1973

Our society is now "mutilated". Some citizens authorize themselves to take away the life of others under all sorts of pretexts, for the sake of vengeance, for a few dollars. Others say: In all conscience, we do not have the right to interfere with the life of criminals. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, what the hon. members do to protect the Canadian people. I would say, without fear of being mistaken, that generally speaking Canadians want the death penalty retained. Some hon. members say: No, we know better than the people; we are better educated, we are more aware, and in short, we are more ready to compromise. And so, with regard to capital punishment, we will be moderate. But I maintain that the general population demands the retention of capital punishment.
So, faced with this alternative, I do not think we have a right to decide according to what we think, even if we claim to be highly aware. How can a few men be more aware than the whole population? That is the question for me, and I will say right away that we have had the abolition of capital punishment for five years, on a trial basis, as a result of a ruling passed by this House. The experience of this trial period has shown a greater increase in the number of murders and other atrocities than has ever been known before in Canadian history. This has been recently, since we abolished capital punishment.
Moreover, we retained capital punishment for those who had taken the lives of policemen or prison guards. Well, there have been not just two policemen or two prison guards killed, but quite a number of them, and the law has not been observed. What has happened to justice? It has been made into injustice. The law existed all right, and laid down these exceptions, but no notice was taken of them. They were passed over by justice.
A handful of men have taken advantage of certain prerogatives to say: We will respect the law to some extent by keeping capital punishment for those who have the nerve to kill a policeman or a prison guard. But when it has come to carrying out justice, justice has gone by the board. There are your men of justice, your moral beings, who lecture everybody and pose as great saviours of the people, great Canadians. But the laws are not respected. According to me, it would be better not to have any. It is better not to talk about those things at all. When we passed this bill, why did we specify those exceptions? Because we thought we were justified in doing so to some extent. Therefore, capital punishment is lawful. It was recognized and it readily is still.
Capital punishment now protects policemen and prison guards, and that protection should be extended to all members of society, because each of them is as important as a prison guard or a policeman. They are human beings as we are, and as are the other citizens.
In Canada, the number of homicides, according to the 1970 statistics, has increased by 60.4 per cent in comparison with 1962. Thus, the crime rate based on the population has increased by 35.3 per cent during the same period and we are told that the death penalty does not frighten anyone, that it would be advisable to abolish it. We are told that it does not increase the number of murders, the
Capital Punishment
crime rate, when we have some statistics that no one can deny.
The number of murders in 1970 has increased by 213.4 per cent over 1962. Thus, the number of attempted murders based on the population has increased by 180 per cent during the same period and we will be told that it is useless, that nothing can be proved, that it is natural, that the law forbids us to kill certain citizens or murderers.
When we deal with a matter such as the death penalty, we must consider the punishment meted out to a criminal. We find awful the punishment given to a criminal, but he has no consideration for people; he commits some atrocity and we find it normal. It is felt that to be human and social, to have the moral accepted, all this should be allowed at society's expenses.
Men of great value are made to disappear, as we have seen in the province of Quebec, and almost nothing is said about it because all the criminals are now being freed and because of the current law and justice everyone is protesting against this kind of punishment applied to citizens and subsequently eliminated.
We must think of punishment and to inflict it to criminals but we should also consider the reasons leading those criminals to commit violations and of their opinion of their punishment. Therefore, if by reinstating capital punishment we succeed in convincing someone not to commit a crime, death penalty should be reestablished as it will contribute to protect society.
If we have the right to kill several thousand people to protect them from an assailant we also have the right to condemn a criminal to protect society.
The death penalty is a necessity; it is a punishment for criminals, a protection for society and not a vengeance for society as stated by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis).
In the same way as a man should protect his life it is also his duty to respect the life of others. It is in that sense that homicide or murder is prohibited by moral law as well as by civil law which must reflect natural law.
It is incumbent on the civil authority to protect citizens by laws and it is its right to enforce the law required by common welfare and the protection of the citizen's life and property.
If police officers have been shot point blank and law is not enforced what is the use of enacting laws, what good is there to be prime minister of a province or of the country? If the laws are not enforced what is the use of this justice which is costing millions of dollars to our fellow citizens? If anything is costly in Canada, it is obviously justice. This is the costliest item for the people and it is always for the sake of great principles of justice that such a thing must be done and that they must spend millions of dollars.
Since the civil authorities must ensure the respect for order in society, they have therefore the right of inflicting punishment and demand repair from those who violate law and order. This is the sanction which completes the law. But can the civil power go so far as to inflict capital punishment?
The political authority has the right to impose capital punishment on those who are guilty of homicide.

May 16, 1973
Capital Punishment
The civil authority has the right to do all that is necessary to serve justice and provide security to citizens. Capital punishment being necessary to provide justice and security to citizens, therefore the civil authority has the right to impose capital punishment and it is its duty to do so.
Punitive justice or justice through revenge demands equality as much as possible between the crime that has been committed and the punishment imposed for such a crime. Now in the case of crimes like homicide, murder, there is no other punishment than capital punishment to create equality between punishment and crime. Therefore, to serve justice, Mr. Speaker, capital punishment is sometimes necessary, which proves the second part of my minor premise.
It is almost impossible to provide for the citizens' security against the acts of certain men without applying the most powerful curbing device that exists against those criminals. Now the most powerful curbing device is capital punishment. Life imprisonment, suggested as a penalty by certain people, is not a curbing device that is strong enough to stop a potential murderer. As a matter of fact, murderers may escape sometimes and thus not serve their sentence. On the other hand, the horrible crime of taking the life of another person is neither sufficiently nor preventively punished through life imprisonment. Capital punishment is a more effective preventive measure since death is the privation of life, the greatest blessing. Capital punishment must be imposed on those who take the life of other people.
Here are some of the objections. It is said that life imprisonment ensures public security and to that, one must answer that life imprisonment ensures security in a certain way, but is life imprisonment sufficient and sufficiently effective? It may be sometimes but it is not always effective. We often had proof of that.
Mr. Speaker, as long as this appendage providing for the hanging of murderers of police officers is not removed, we shall be accomplices, voluntarily or not. Legalized, institutionalized murder and death voluntarily given, either by an individual or by a just society that wants to punish them remains a crime and an even more serious crime when it is committed by individuals who have been able to think about their actions.
We have received hundreds of folders and citizens have been sending us protest letters requesting that capital punishment be maintained. For instance, I have with me a report from the newspaper Le Droit of December 5, 1969, and I quote:
Capital punishment is necessary to protect society.
During this interview Parliament member and lawyer Remi Paul stated the reasons against abolition of capital punishment.
He is one man who speaks against abolition openly and proudly.
I have also with me an article rewritten by a former judge, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) who, through newspapers, invited people to write to the federal government and request it not to abolish the death penalty. A lengthy summary has been made of that and I wonder whether the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe will have the courage to rise and repeat what he has been

saying and asking from the population for a few years. I wonder whether he will follow his leader and raise his arm when his leader will raise his, or whether he will assume his true responsibilities.
I have with me another press article which I quote:
Dramatic increase in murders in Quebec since 1961 (C. Wagner)-
-attributed to the abolition of capital punishment.
There is a whole page, Mr. Speaker, which I will not read.
I have also received a letter from the Quebec Federation of Retail Services, addressed as follows:
To all members of the Canadian House of Commons who are from the province of Quebec Dear member of Parliament:
The Quebec Federation of Retail Services, which groups seven professional associations of retailers from various sectors of the retail trade, wishes to inform you that, upon consideration of the problem of the death penalty, our administrative council has decided in favour of its retention.
We have received thousands of letters like that one, and yet it is said that the population knows nothing about it.
The member for Saint-Hyacinthe certainly knows something about it.
Other associations have written to me; to quote the Civil Service Association of Canada:
As a member of Parliament, you will be invited during the present session to vote on the matter of the abolition of the death penalty in Canada. The Civil Service Association would not normally concern itself with so controversial a matter of public politics. We would consider that our members prefer to decide about this matter in the manner which the government seems to intend to adopt in Parliament, leaving each person free to make his decision individually.
In this specific case, however, our Association has, as an organization, an important interest in one aspect of the problem. We refer to the abolition of the death penalty for murderers of prison employees or guards during attempts at escape or any other incident in which a victim is legally carrying out his duties.
Mr. Speaker, I shall not read them all. Members of parliament are asked to retain the death penalty, at any cost. We receive any number of letters like that one; all hon. members must have received some.
I quote: "Young conservatives in favour of retention." It is strange to notice that the Progressive Conservatives now accept the proposals of the government for abolishing the death penalty for another five years. It was suspended for five years and that should be good enough to know what happened: statistics are there to prove it; the number of murders increased alarmingly over that period and even though I am no "smart aleck", I do not want to carry things too far either.
Conscientiously, I should greatly prefer that none should have to go through such atrocities but we are here, Mr. Speaker to deal justice, to enlighten the people, to enact legislation protecting the people. They need protection and I believe that on the whole Progressive Conservative hon. members and Liberal members as well are prepared to maintain the elimination of a capital punishment
May 16, 1973

for another trial period of five years, claiming that it is barbarous to take a citizen's life.
In many countries, Mr. Speaker, this would not be tolerated. In several countries there are even no inquiries and bums are done away with, who bring evil and discord into society and the lives of respectable citizens.
Mr. Speaker, I should have much to say, but since others want to participate in the debate I shall say that for our part we shall be voting against Bill C-2, an Act to amend the Criminal Code.
The Criminal Code exists, Mr. Speaker. It should be amended, but in order to protect people and not to further encourage the atrocities we are now experiencing.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we are invited to vote upon the motion for second reading of Bill C-2, I would like to say a few words about this matter which has given rise to many debates and votes for a few years.
I had the opportunity of taking the floor twice in this House, when bills were introduced in 1966 and 1967. In 1967, the House passed a bill which suspended capital punishment, except in cases of murders of police officers or penitentiary guards on duty, for a five-year period. This five-year period was over at the end of 1972 and today, the government found it advisable to introduce in this House a bill that is similar to that which was passed in 1967, thus extending for another five-year period the abolishment of capital punishment, except in cases I referred to earlier.
I intend to say a few words, without passion, without emotion and on my own behalf only. I do not intend to convince anybody, and I do not think that I could succeed in do so. I was told that this was an emotional issue; probably there will not be any more important matter before Parliament for a long time.
I listened carefully today to the passionless and emotionless speech of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). I take his word and I am sure of it, when he says that each case was or will be fairly assessed. However, I must admit that it might be more difficult to convince the right hon. Prime Minister about the advisability of capital punishment. I am expressing a personal view but I suggest that the Prime Minister is right when he says that each case must be considered or will be considered in all fairness.
I listened to the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) whose speech, I must admit, was very vague. We do not really know what will happen during the third reading of this bill after it has been considered in committee.
As for myself, I intend to inform hon. members of my decision when motions on second and third reading will be put. I plan to vote in favour of this legislation on second reading since I believe with certain exceptions that a bill should be considered thoroughly and on its merit.
When this bill comes back before the House I will make my decision, that is to say that if it is not amended so as to propose the complete abolition of capital punishment I will vote against it. Let me explain. I think that those who
Capital Punishment
heard my speeches in the past know that it is not an emotional issue for me. When I opposed certain bills in the past I explained why I was opposing them and I explained specially that I was concerned with other aspects such as parole, criminal records, rehabilitation of inmates, trials and preliminary inquiries. Some improvements have been brought about since then in the field of criminal records, bails, trials, preliminary inquiries and many other areas.
However, Mr. Speaker, I now consider the problem of abolition or retention as settled. The facts are there to prove it. I do not think that this government-and it is my personal opinion-nor any other government which could be called upon to run this country in the immediate future would ever send anybody to the gallows. So I consider the problem as solved. We had better stop talking about it and be realistic and know what to do after. We must then ensure that inmates are rehabilitated when possible.
Some people talk about revenge and protecting society. I have a lot of respect for those who make such arguments; it is their right to do so and it is not my intention to blame them for it. However, I for one think that there is only one thing that counts, that is what we are going to do with the inmates after their detention. I do not believe in those arguments of deterrence. As the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said a moment ago, the statistics in that field are more or less good and we will never know the number of persons who committed or did not commit a murder because there was abolition or not. But one thing is sure: the general public does feel that no one will be hanged either under the present government or under the next governments whatever the party in power. So we must reassure the public once and for all and tell them that abolition is a fact.
And what are we going to do now? Later, for any reason, if Parliament sees fit, it will introduce another legislation and restore capital punishment if needed. We must make up our mind now, once and for all. But to say that they will introduce that legislation to have more statistics, this is a unbelievable joke. Everybody knows that within the next five years, nobody will be sentenced to death. Some may believe it, but I do not. It is not a way to gather statistics.
I have listened with considerable interest to the leader of the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for York South, who had the courage to say this afternoon that he at least was not satisfied with this bill; he saw a compromise in it and he had the courage to say so.
I consider it takes courage to settle the issue once and for all and to abolish capital punishment. Something must be done. For instance, in trying to convince us or the population, as have done some hon. members or other people who do not sit in this House, some persons give the following argument: As a compromise, of course, to try to have this bill passed, which I consider as inefficient, we will now arrange so that those who under this bill are sentenced to death for qualified murder stay in prison 20 years, without getting out and without remission. This is barbarism.
I have studied the problem of penitentiaries and of their inmates, Mr. Speaker, because I have always been interested in this and I think a good many hon. members in this House know it, and I can say, of course, that a good many

May 16, 1973
Capital Punishment
persons who know the problem agree with me that if we let someone in a penitentiary without any hope of getting out for 20 years, he will grow crazy or commit suicide.
I know, Mr. Speaker, the case of people who were sentenced to death and were imprisoned for life, for manslaughter for instance.
I can say that if, after 10 years, a person is not rehabilitated and ready to be sent back to society with the necessary safeguards, he will never be. I think we must have in mind what 10 years in prison can represent. I have never been in jail. But we must imagine what it is like.
I know someone, Mr. Speaker, who has been serving his life sentence for 9 years. I think that this person is now rehabilitated. I can be wrong but I think he is. But it is not in the ninth year that he is rehabilitated; it started as early as the first or second year, because it must be understood that if a person is found guilty, he is in a state of mind that prompts him to live in general in a world which does not facilitate his rehabilitation on the first day of imprisonment.
That person, often after one year or two, comes to realize that it is possible, and he takes the necessary means, with the help of a psychiatrist, to rehabilitate himself. But if he were told tomorrow morning that he has no chance to get out after 10 or 11 years, then he would stop being a case for rehabilitation. I am convinced of that.
When I hear people in this House or elsewhere say, always for the sake of compromise or for other reasons-I say "for the sake of compromise" because I believe that is the reason-that criminals will be imprisoned for 20 years and that the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs will amend the bill to let the population know that those people will serve their sentence for 20 years, that it will be impossible for them to come out of prison before that, I think one makes another error, Mr. Speaker. So, in my humble opinion, there will be no more joking.
If the matter were referred to a committee, if a bill advocating the complete abolition of the death penalty were considered, I would be the first to support it. I know that my views on the subject are well known, but those who have read my speeches must realize that I have changed. I do not say that there is no deterrent, but I do not believe in revenge. I believe along with others-and the Prime Minister referred to this this afternoon-that there is a punitive factor and the punishment, it must be admitted after all, can be adequate. What can be done about it? When one drives through a red light, a $20 fine is levied. If someone steals $50, $5,000, or a million he will be punished accordingly. Evidence shows generally that a sentence is somewhat suited to the crime, though mistakes are always possible.
We must admit, and this is quite simplistic,-to be consistent with our opinions-that when a person deliberately kills another, it is said that he who voluntarily kills deserves an adequate punishment, which is death. Let us forget about this and stop talking about this problem. We shall never find a solution. We shall never succeed in convincing 22 million Canadians that abolition or retention is necessary. It is impossible.
If tomorrow morning a three-year old girl is murdered for example, people will be shocked and will say: Let him

hang! But two or three years later, when the accused is found guilty and the decision is made to hang him, then people will say: It is most unfortunate. After all, it will not bring the child back to life.
We shall thus never find a solution, Mr. Speaker. Then, let the government introduce a bill in favour of abolition and with full knowledge of the facts, honestly and sincerely, let us vote on this question.
Then, I would vote for abolition. I said that I would not try to convince anyone; it is the only thing that I can say. I have tried to convince people by saying: That is enough, let us abolish capital punishment and then make sure that prisoners get what they deserve. When we day "what they deserve", it means that when they are in prison, we should take steps to keep them there, and I am not casting reflections on any member in this connection. Let us see to it that those who can be rehabilitated will be and that those who cannot be rehabilitated stay in prison.
In this way, the population will know where it stands and we shall live in a climate of security rather than uncertainty. In fact, this climate of uncertainty exists in the public as well as in penitentiaries, which is demoralizing for everyone and does not help at all to solve the problem. This does not help society either because it is much better protected when we know where we are going and when there is no procrastination, when there is no last minute compromise which often does no credit to those who makes it.
With this, Mr. Speaker, I end my remarks which I had hoped would be shorter and which, I trust, will not have been too painful to listen to.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join some of my colleagues who have said that it is unfortunate that we are required to debate the capital punishment issue at this particular time in this particular parliament. It is unfortunate for a number of reasons. If not the most important, certainly the first reason, is that capital punishment is not the issue that we should be considering. It is but one of the problems that plague our total penal system, as the debate of last night indicated. But in this debate we must restrict ourselves to the issue of capital punishment.
It has been characteristic of this House, during my short career here, that we legislate from one crisis to the next crisis. This is stop gap legislation. We should be addressing ourselves now to the real problems of the country-the economic issues-which include unemployment, inflation, unemployment insurance and income tax. Any one of these problems is more serious than the one that is presently under debate.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, the Criminal Code already contains provisions which, although ignored, deal with murder. But we must address ourselves to this most perplexing bill which, if passed, will be a victory for abolitionists and murderers, although it will still permit capital punishment, and which, if defeated, will still be a victory for abolitionists and murderers because, de facto, we have
May 16, 1973

already said goodbye to capital punishment anyway, because the government won't enforce the law.
But, Mr. Speaker, this is a bad bill. It is so confusing that our Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) and Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) who, on the one hand, say they are abolitionists, on the other hand say that they will support the bill even though it provides for capital punishment.
Much has been said in this debate, and I do not want to be repetitive. At this point I must say that I shall find myself compelled to vote against the government's bill. This is not necessarily because I am overwhelmingly in favour of capital punishment but because the bill does not provide the Canadian people with the protection that I deem necessary. I stress protection because that is my No. 1 concern-the protection of the innocent members of society, people like our wives and children. Abolitionists overlook this most important aspect and express pity for the murderers. They say, "But you cannot bring back a murder victim." I say "we want protection while we are alive".
The abolitionists point to statistics and say that capital punishment is not a deterrent to murder, and so it should be abolished. They point to the statistics to support their claim, but we all know that statistics can be used to prove anything that the statistician wants to prove. Let me give you some examples.
Statistics Canada, on January 19 of this year, issued a report revealing that the average number of murders during the years 1961 to 1967 inclusive was 222 per year. During the four years after the temporary ban was instituted the average number of murders was 376 per year, reaching a peak of 422 in 1971. Certainly, these figures show that the suspension of capital punishment was no deterrent to murder. My colleague from Calgary North has reminded us that the deterrent effect can never be measured accurately because we do not know how many people would have committed murder if there had been no death penalty. But I am not worried about whether a murderer fears being put to death. I am worried about protection of the innocent.
The abolitionists say that retentionists want revenge. I am not concerned with revenge. Probably full life, or even 25 years in prison is a punishment worse than death. I am concerned with protection. You will hear it said that imprisonment will provide the protection. I ask for whom? Certainly protection will not be provided for the prison guards or for the public after one of these murderers escapes.
The bill we are asked to pass provides that the killing of a policeman or prison guard is punishable by death, but other premeditated and violent killing is not. Is this the leadership the people deserve from our government?
You probably also hear it said that the courts can err and the wrong man could be executed. Mr. Speaker, the chance of this happening is so remote that it hardly bears consideration. The courts of our land today have so many safeguards, so many checks and balances, that the risk of being wrongfully executed is hardly measurable, certainly not when it is compared with the risks we all take every day when we get out of bed and go into the streets. It could even be described as a non-existent risk. But the
Capital Punishment
abolitionists do not consider the risk of murder to our innocent citizens.
There is another type of protection that bears mention at this time. A close associate of mine, who is a skilled courtroom lawyer, has said that if his wife or child were murdered and the murderer were later released he would search out and kill that murderer. He does not attempt to justify what he would do, and he fully realizes that his action would be reprehensible, but he would be unable to stop himself. He needs protection just as much as his loved ones. If we do not give society the protection it demands, we shall find ourselves returning to the days when the quickest and the strongest ruled, to the old doctrine of might is right. People will ignore the law if the law ignores them.
I have said many things about protection because protection has long been the concern of every member of every society. Society found long ago that some of its members acted in an anti-social way, and that the majority required protection from the few. They established police forces to provide this protection. In this most important debate, the chiefs of all our police forces are urging us to retain capital punishment. Are we to ignore the men who are hired to protect us?
The aims of the abolitionists are admirable-to murderers! Frequently, the abolitionists are people who say they are concerned with helping mankind. But they seem to be obsessed with helping the few-the guilty few-instead of helping the many-the innocent many. It is time these people began to be concerned about preserving the cream and throwing away the scum!
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) today spoke of passion killing. These would be manslaughter charges and not capital murder, anyway. But the hon. member says in so many words that he would let the hired killer remain alive to escape and kill again.
Since my election, I, like the others in this House, have heard hundreds of opinions expressed by constituents and others. We have heard the scriptures quoted by both sides in the debate, but I am convinced that the vast majority of Canadians want a return to capital punishment, though they want it for various reasons. It is true that some are vengeful or have other reasons, but the single, most moving reason is protection, and my direction is clear. I think the innocent citizens expect their elected representatives to give them the protection of the law, and I am opposed to this bill because it does not give the protection demanded.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I should like to agree with the views of the previous speaker, my colleague the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Clark) regarding why there are many more important topics and issues to be debated here at this time, such as our general economic problems and the drastic rise in food prices. Also, there has been so much said on the subject of capital punishment in the last few days, months and indeed years, in this country and others, that one would suppose there is nothing left to say. It seems to me, however, not only due to my own strong

May 16, 1973
Capital Punishment
feelings, but the personal contact I have had with many people regarding this matter, that no one person has really summed up all the real issues.
Now, I am not going to pretend to be the guiding light as far as a solution is concerned-far from it. I want to merely state, Mr. Speaker, what I, personally, believe is the true feeling and belief of the majority of our society, a society that is not sick or degenerated, but a society trying to live in harmony and peace. Under normal circumstances, it could be called the silent majority, but when it comes to this issue of capital punishment, it is a society far from being silent.
Mr. Speaker, I have stated on numerous occasions to my constituents of High Park-Humber Valley in Toronto, because capital punishment is such an individually emotional issue, that when the vote came up, I would vote on this matter as the majority of my constituents would want me to vote. In that regard, I have recently sent out a questionnaire to my constituents and have had a response of 83 per cent for capital punishment, 12 per cent against, and 5 per cent undecided. Now I can vote on this matter not only as my constituents would want me to, but also as my conscience directs me.
We remember that in April, 1966, an attempt was made to achieve complete abolition, but it was rejected on a free vote in this House. In 1967, the same parliament passed for a five-year trial, a law which was a compromise and which abolished hanging for all but the murderers of prison guards and policemen. But was one man hanged? No. The government has not only made a mockery of the courts, but of their own laws. This law, as we all know, expired at the end of 1972. But murders in Canada continue. I have some statistics, though I really do not want to dwell on statistics as such. One statistic supplied by Statistics Canada shows that from 1961, when the capital murder rate in Canada was one in every 100,000 Canadians, it rose to 2.3 murders in every 100,000 in 1970.
In Great Britain, as we know, capital punishment was abolished in 1965. Four years prior to the bill, 71 murders took place in Great Britain. During the four years after the abolishing of capital punishment there were 161 convictions on murder charges. This figures would have been much higher had the courts not charged dozens of murderers with manslaughter instead. These statistics speak for themselves, Mr. Speaker.
The profound question, then, that immediately faces hon. members in the twenty-ninth parliament is, are we in favour of the death penalty for murder or are we not? It is often contended that too much sympathy is shown the criminals, too little thought given to the victims, to the families and personal communities of which they were members. This contention I would not seek to refute. It's truth is too often only too clear. If it is argued that other considerations are more important, it is not argued that this one is unimportant, or does not deserve more practical weight than it has been given.
It is widely held that a principal aim of the whole system of criminal justice should be reform of the criminal, that the convicted person deserves the right and the opportunity to make a new start in life. That also, is not being contradicted, except by this consideration: that we are concerned here with capital crimes, that what may be

valid for 99 in every 100 criminals is not necessarily valid for the hundredth. Even if every dog were entitled to his bite, the rule would not apply to a mad dog. Therefore, once again we ask ourselves the question-should a man who has wilfully killed another man, himself be killed?
Historically, this question has been asked of those living after the event. The prosecuting attorney pleads it in his implacable argument before the judge and jury. The defense attorney denies it in his impassioned plea for the life of the murderer. The judge juggles the question in his summing up to the jury, and the jury deliberates on it, sometimes in anguish, sometimes in great clarity of mind.
Yet in all that has been written and said on the subject of capital punishment, seldom has anyone questioned what the victim would say about it if only he could. And, after all, equally with his murderer, the victim would have a right to speak in the matter of his own death and its punishment. Supposing the intended victim of a premeditated murder were to know in a flash of insight exactly what was in the mind of his assailant. Suppose everything were equal. Suppose the intended victim had a gun in his hand at the same instant as his murderer approached him with a gun in his hand. What would be the inalienable right of the threatened man? What would you do, if you were the intended victim? Would you simply stand there and allow yourself to be shot through the heart? If so, you would voluntarily relinquish your equality before the law and your right to the love of the land. Would you turn and run? Then, you would be a coward. Or, would you employ equal force to his and shoot him dead?
The trouble is, the rights of the victim are often overlooked in the hurly-burly of the trial of his murderer. All of the attention is fixed on the plight of the man on trial. Safe in their own comfortable homes, remote from the confrontation which took place at the moment of a man's death, people are prone in the intervening months to sympathize with this living man who is, after all, one of them and must merit mercy. They forget that the dead victim received neither sympathy nor mercy. There is generally only one recognized sanction proposed as an alternative to capital punishment for crimes of a capital nature, guaranteed lengthy prison terms. Long prison terms, however, may justly be criticized as being repulsive, as being punishment of the sort condemned in the language of the Constitution of the United States of America as "cruel and unusual". A sensitive society must shrink from the infliction of such prolonged punishment as it should shrink from torture. In most cases, it is not a punishment which fits the crime, but punishment which balances slow psychic death against the sudden killing.
Those who speak or think "humanity" must forget long prison terms; a person who has spent many years behind bars and concrete walls degenerates beyond recognition into a class close to vegetation. Let us become humane by not allowing our laws to let humans become vegetables. There are secondary reasons as well for this position, such as the cost of feeding, clothing and housing men and women whose proved relationship to society has been one of violent antagonism, basic opposition to the values and standards accepted by the community. A large group of fellow citizens should not be subjected to the difficult,
May 16, 1973

dangerous and demeaning task of serving as keepers of the enemies of society, who have behaved like brute beasts.
Now, what really should be considered as a capital crime? Well, in Canada as in other countries there has been at work a steady refinement of definition, a narrowing of meaning, as to the crimes for which capital punishment should be imposed. Much of the process has been good; in part it has been extreme. Some comments should be made about the sorts of considerations which must weigh with parliament and the courts. There is a justifiable distinction, but one which it is very difficult to draw, between the premeditated murder and the act of sudden passion. It is surely reasonable to assume that if a person carried a lethal weapon to the place where he kills, he must have forseen the possibility of using it.
The tendency to regard somewhat leniently the person who commits a crime under the influence of alcohol or drugs is one which it is difficult to justify in the great majority of cases which come before the courts. Even when the use of intoxicants and drugs has not deliberately preceded, as an act of preparation, the commission of the crime, it is clear that in many cases the offender must have been aware of the likely effects of their use. Such a person should be held responsible for his choice and its consequences. One who has made a wrong choice of this sort and killed, has destroyed his own case for leniency on the grounds of possible penitence and reform. How can he be trusted again to have freedom of choice in the world, even after 15 or 20 years?
There has been little discussion of capital crimes other than murder. This is unfortunate, because a comparison of crimes can be helpful in evaluating their seriousness. Hanging for rape had disappeared in Canada before the penalty was removed from the Criminal Code, partly because of the extraordinary difficulty of proving guilt. But, as is the case with other crimes of violence, there is an upward trend in the rate of offences. The justification for retaining the supreme penalty as an alternative is that in some cases of psychopathic murder, the results for the victim are perhaps even more terrible than the results of other kinds of murder. It would be a declaration by society of its code of values, if nothing else, if the capital alternative were restored in the statute.
Sea piracy has been rated a capital offence, and the same reasons now require that air piracy be classified in the same way. The pirate, by sea or air, for the most part operates outside the area of national law and police action, and by violence or threat of violence he takes over the command of a fragile carrier, endangering the safety of passengers and crew. He also, potentially, ranks among the most dangerously anti-socials who commit wholesale murder.
Hard drug pushers, not users, could possibly rate as the worst killers in our society and should come under the capital crimes law. They pick on the weak, the confused, the young, the frustrated,, and they spread a disease worse than cancer, a disease that could not only ruin an empire but, indeed, mankind. The growing cult of violence may make additions to the list of capital crimes desirable. The use of explosives, with their capacity for mass murder,
Capital Punishment
makes ordinary citizens on the street or going about their business more vulnerable to the whims of merciless killers than has been the case in the past.
Well, Mr. Speaker, it is more than clear by now that the majority of my constituents and I are totally in favour of bringing back capital punishment as soon as possible in order to save whatever dignity and freedom there is left in our lives and our own society. There are, however, two final points which I should like to make at this time. First, let us be humane by not allowing a human being to rot in jail over a 20 year or more term, as I have stated; and let us civilize ourselves by imposing the death penalty in a more humane fashion than hanging. There are up-to-date medical facilities and drugs that could be utilized without having to make a production of the execution.
Unfortunately, there are in this country still too many people who believe the death penalty for murder is a cruel and inhuman punishment for a man or woman convicted of such a crime. These people, it appears, have no regard for the victim or the victim's family, as I have said. That and the attitude of the federal cabinet during the five year ban which has just expired makes me bristle. We must realize that men and women "hyped" by speed and armed with weapons walk our streets with violence in their minds and murder in their hearts. You and I walk these same streets unarmed, protected only by the men recruited to keep law and order; and when these men give their lives while protecting our lives and our property, who pays? Does the law of the land demand payment? Yes, it does.
Who, then, should have the right to abrogate that law? The federal cabinet, in an aberration for which there is no sensible reason and which cannot be justified, does and has exercised that right repeatedly. It is time to re-examine this masochistic trait. We teach people that the age of maturity is 18. If a person, after he or she reaches that age, chooses to operate outside the mainstream of society and is convicted of killing a man who maintains the law of the land, you cannot justify commutation. You are doing an injustice to those who live within the law and to those who maintain it. A killer has no right to inflict his presence on this society after he has been sentenced to death for murder. For if he lives, he is living proof that society has no desire to protect itself or protect those hired to protect lives and property. To let him live makes a mockery of the law, makes a mockery of those who enacted the legislation and of those who elected the representatives who passed the legislation.

subsubtopic: REINSTATEMENT OF LAW RELATING TO CAPITAL PUNISHMENT THAT EXISTED PRIOR TO DECEMBER 30, 1972
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am deeply moved as I participate in the debate on Bill C-2 calling for a five-year extension of the abolishment of capital punishment. The matter is one of great import, since it relates directly to man's greatest possession, which is life.
Because of the sacred nature of human life I believe legislation should reflect this in reality by applying the maximum penalty to those who deliberately violate the principle.
We live within a society and I believe we all agree that this society should reach a very high level of civilization and that our laws should contribute to achieving this goal

May 16, 1973
Capital Punishment
by ensuring a maximum of security for members of this society. People are entitled to normal protection, and it is up to the government to provide it. That is why we should pass legislation to ensure public security and also to punish those who jeopardize the liberty and security of others.
The many escapes from our prisons and penitentiaries do not foster a feeling of security among the people. It is the government's responsibility, therefore, to ensure the security of members of society by enacting legislation to increase their feeling of being protected against law-breakers.
We live in a century when each and every one, in his own way, proclaims the right to be free. Freedom is not only for the individual, but for his neighbours. Therefore, whoever takes his neighbour's life harms the other in his life, in his right to live. And in our modern society the tendency is to treat criminals just as though taking one's neighbour's life were not a crime.
When we consult our voters on the matter of the abolition of capital punishment, we see that many of them are worried about the rise in crime in this country, of mass escapes, of parole and sentences that are commuted by the executive, all of which goes to reduce the public's confidence in the judiciary.
The government must therefore provide better protection, so as to create a feeling of security among the population, a feeling which is becoming dangerously rare nowadays. Every day in newspapers and magazines and on radio and television, people are being literally flooded with news of the possible adoption of all kinds of measures to make things easier for criminals, and they might well wonder if criminals really exist, and if society is really protected.
Young people should be better informed about what the police force really is; they should be taught that a policeman is first and foremost the citizens' friend and not a scourge, that his job is sometimes unrewarding, that it is his duty to ensure individual safety, to which end he must enforce the law.
When the Criminal Code was amended to abolish the death penalty, with two exceptions, it was for a trial period of five years. During the trial period, a number of policemen and prison guards were murdered, and certain people were accused, given a fair trial, found guilty and condemned to death. However, how many of those found guilty have been executed?
I have here a reply that was given in the House to a question that I had put on the order paper, which shows clearly that the executive changes sentences passed by the judiciary, rendering inoperative a law whose implementation we are now asked to extend for another five-year period.
The question and the answer can be found in Hansard for March 6, 1972, page 535. I quote:
1.	(a) How many death sentences were imposed by the courts from January 1, 1967 to December 15, 1971 (b) how many sentences were executed (c) how many sentences were commuted?

Here is the answer from the hon. Jean-Pierre Goyer (Solicitor General):
1.	(a) Thirteen, (b) None; (c) Eleven.
So, 11 times out of 13 the government changed the sentence of the court. Here is the second part of the question:
2.	For what crime was each of these persons sentenced to death?
Here is the answer:
2.	Murder, in each case.
Here is the third part of the question:
3.	(a) What are the names of those sentenced to death who have received a commutation ...
Then follows the list and I will not bother to enumerate those persons. The dates of commutations through orders in council are the following: January 4 1968, eight orders in council allowing eight commutations of sentences. The cabinet is proceeding in series. The three others bear different dates.
Canadian have the right to expect that the law be obeyed and that the crime be punished according to penalties provided in the law.
Any normal human being is upset when he hears of a murder, that the life of a human being has been taken out of malice. This is why I understand the feeling of horror that moves the majority of Canadians to want that a crime as horrifying as capital murder be punished.
I understand that the human justice process is not absolute and that we could always make a mistake. This is not only the case for charges under the Criminal Code but also under the Civil Code, yet they continue to apply penalties provided under the Civil Code.
After a just trial, Mr. Speaker, when all known means to find the truth have been used and an accused has been convicted of having taken the life of his fellow citizen, is there really a compensation measure more just than capital punishment?
Let us take as an example the case of an individual who deliberately makes a device to explode a bomb in a public place, and by the way causes the death of one or several persons and then, it is demonstrated beyond all doubt that he is the criminal. Can we, in all conscience, allow this crime to go unpunished? What would then say the children of a mother who would find death in such circumstances?
I feel that it is just that capital punishement be maintained in the case of the murder of a policemen or a prison guard. The life of a mother or a father should be just as valuable because, as far as the mother is concerned, she is the gardien and the educator of her children, and as far as the father is concerned, no matter what his profession, he is the bread winner for his wife and children.
Why one law for the rich and another for the poor? Is the life of the bank clerk, the working man, the road employee not as useful to his family?
Let us be logical and to be so, the partisans of the abolition of the death penalty should avoid suggesting that some reservations should be made. They should demand the abolition of the death penalty for treachery and crimes committed under the National Defence Act.
May 16, 1973

Those crimes are nevertheless subject to the death penalty, because they are crimes against the state which is lifeless. If it is fair to protect state representatives, why not protect the life of people who make up the state?
Some hon. members who approve the abolition of the death penalty have referred to judicial errors. However, we all know that hanging applies to capital murders only, when there is no shadow of a doubt that the accused is really guilty.
If the minister is convinced that the maintenance of the death penalty for the murder of police officers and prison guards will have a deterrent effect, that penalty should logically have a deterrent effect in other cases.
I am convinced that it is essential to protect the life of police officers and prison guards by maintaining the death penalty. Therefore, it would be proper to protect the life of young girls threatened with murder and assault. Is there a difference between the murder of a police officer during a bank hold-up and that of a young girl victim of a rape by a sexual deviate?
Who was not astounded and indignant when we learned last fall the murder of two gamekeepers in Quebec? I had known one of them for many years: he was a model employee and father and a honest citizen.
Of what right have the killers of these people availed themselves to act this way? Even though we live in a society which prides itself for being progressive, can we really let such crimes go unpunished? Would that really be showing advanced civic-mindedness to leave injustice and violence without any punishment?
The state is in some way responsible for the alarming crime increase in Canada by letting movie theatres and television stations show several times a day to millions of easily influenced people pictures in which men and women are being stabbed, shot, strangled, poisoned, drowned or handled roughly in all sorts of manners. The state should be concerned with the sacred nature of life and deal severely with the lack of respect for life shown by telecasts and movies that have such an influence on young Canadians.
As representatives of the people in this house, we have some very serious responsibilities and must discharge them to the best of our judgment. I for one, that is what I want to do, even if I do respect the opinions of my colleagues. However, I must also take into account the will of the majority of the people I represent.
We must not only have penal laws, but must above all create a social climate favoring a better understanding of the individuals that make up society. There should be more justice in the sharing of ressources, in order to allow each and everyone to satisfy his vital needs.
Finally, it would also be desirable to emphasize our rehabilitation programs for inmates. The entire society should also be better disposed towards them, once they are released, so they do not feel rejected, and such an attitude would help prevent relapse.
I think also that our laws should be more generous in the matter of compensation for the victims of those who have broken the law, which, in my opinion, would be a proof of generosity; it would contribute towards making
Capital Punishment
the masses more aware of the need for doing more in the way of rehabilitating those who have had the misfortune of erring.
We wonder whether the death penalty is a deterrent; yet, I am convinced that the amendment to the Criminal Code authorizing the use of the breathlizer gave good results. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the holder of a driving licence who wants to keep it has had to be much more careful about the use of alcoholic beverages in the last few years than previously, which proves that the measure has had the expected results, that is, that people are more careful.
The same reasoning can apply with regard to the demerit point system adopted in Quebec. I have repeatedly noticed that drivers are more careful and respectful of the law. That is why I see preventive measures in those sanctions.
As I see it, the best solution to the problem of capital punishment, the most democratic one, would be to hold a referendum. I hope some day the government will take the necessary steps to introduce a legislation authorizing one. We would then have the population participate in a decision in which it is interested.
As for now, Mr. Speaker, I have to make my own decision as a member of this House. I will do so very freely and will, quite objectively, vote against Bill C-2.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say, through you, to all hon. members that the subject which we are debating has been one that has caused me a great amount of concern for a number of years. I think I speak for all other hon. members when I say that the anguish with which I have at times in the past approached this question convinces me that the vast majority of my fellow men, who are probably rational and sensitive creatures, have also approached the question with a certain degree of anguish. No matter what I am going to say in the next few minutes, I want to assure all hon. members that I commence these remarks with the profoundest regard for the position taken by other members in this House, even though I may differ with some of them.
I believe the first point that I must make is that this is not an abolition bill. This bill is a bill to hang the murderers of policemen and prison guards. It may at best be called a partial abolition bill, but it is not an abolition bill. I think this point has to be made for two reasons. I have received a great deal of correspondence on the whole subject. Those who are for abolition have written to me in the belief that this is an abolition bill. I notice-I must be fair about this-that I have had fewer of those letters lately.
It is because so many people have gone into this whole issue over the last year on the assumption that the issue would be abolition or retention that there is still in the country a degree of confusion. It is hard to disagree with my position that this is not an abolition bill. If that is so, then one must ask oneself where is the logic in advancing the arguments that have been most eloquently advanced

May 16, 1973
Capital Punishment
in favour of the abolition of capital punishment, and yet not apply them in the two areas where the bill still provides for the taking of the life of the transgressor.
The other evening, on Monday night, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) spoke in this debate. No member who was in this House could doubt the sincerity of his remarks, least of all myself. But when he finished I asked, through you, Mr. Speaker, whether he would allow a question, to which he graciously consented. For the record in this debate and in this speech of mine, I want to read an extract from Hansard for May 14, page 3739. This was my question:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize to the minister because I did not hear all of his speech, but I wonder if he would be good enough to answer a question which I think troubles a number of us who are very sympathetic to much of what he has said. If one is advocating the abolition of capital punishment on the grounds that the minister has stated-and other hon. members have spoken along the same line-where is the logical distinction between hanging a frightened man who runs out of a bank and shoots a policeman, and not hanging a man who shoots the prime minister, or who may engage in the diabolical business of killing people for the underground.
I meant "underworld".
I would be interested to hear the minister's views on this particular problem.
The minister answered in this way:
Mr. Speaker, I very much appreciate that question. I think the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) will appreciate from my remarks that I did not attempt to distinguish in any logical way why one particular type of murder rather than another should have capital punishment attached to it.
I quote that because what else could the Minister of Justice say? There is, in my view, no logical distinction. It has been said: "Well, the bill has to be the way it is, otherwise we would never get it through the House of Commons; we would have to continue the law as it became at the end of the year and have capital and non-capital offences". I am led to understand that this was the same argument that was put up five years ago. I was not a member five years ago, but I did wonder then at the logic of it. I have not been persuaded in the intervening years that what I regarded as illogical a few years ago has become logical with the passage of time.
I listened with great interest this afternoon to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He advanced, again in an eloquent way, his personal feelings about the death penalty. I respect what the Prime Minister said. He takes the view-many people take this view-that to have the death penalty is, in itself, something that ought to be abhorrent to a sensitive and civilized community. I know there are others who do not agree, but I respect that position. If that is so, how then can one escape the logical next step, which is that it is just as wrong on a moral basis-this was really the basis on which the Prime Minister put his remarks-to hang a frightened young man who shoots a police officer as he runs out of a bank? In case anybody misunderstand me, I do not justify what the boy does because he is frightened, but there is such inconsistency in hanging that young man and not hanging people who have done and are likely to do more diabolical things that I think it confounds the public's acceptance of the basic logic of what we are doing.

I have heard hon. members here say that it is proven that the death penalty is not a deterrent. I have heard other hon. members say they believe it is. I am more inclined to believe that statistics prove nothing about capital punishment. An intelligent editorial in The Globe and Mail of November 30, 1970 headed in those exact words "Statistics prove nothing about capital punishment", pretty well sums up my own feeling. In that article there is a reference to a study by the University of Toronto Centre of Criminology. Let me quote from the editorial:
The study, written by Barbara Schloss and N. A. Giesbrecht, concentrates on the 10-year period ending with 1970 and concludes that it is impossible to tell at this stage what effect abolition of the death penalty for murderers of civilians has had. It also concludes that it is impossible to define trends in the murder of police officers and prison guards.
The study may be right, but I have not seen anything that convinces me there is statistical proof for the proposition that capital punishment is a deterrent or vice versa. I happen to think it is a deterrent but I concede as I say that I cannot find proof one way or the other. It may well be that what is a deterrent for me may not be a deterrent for somebody else. I also note that capital punishment may not be a deterrent to all people in every circumstance. If we accept the argument put forward by those who have been speaking in favour of the bill, that deterrent is not a reason for applying capital punishment because capital punishment is not a deterrent in itself. Again, I ask where is the logic for hanging the boy who runs out of a bank and shoots a policeman?
We think of the killing of a prison guard as something which must be heinous, and perhaps planned. The person is waiting at the corner to throttle the guard. I put it to you that it could easily happen under very different circumstances. It could happen in a prison riot where, in the panic and confusion of the moment, some foolish man hits a guard too hard across the back of the head, not meaning to kill him. Perhaps he meant only to grip him or tie him up, but still death can result. The proponents of this bill would then hang that person. Again, I do not see the logic of this, because if hanging is no deterrent, and this is what is said, why hang him?
There is a basic problem when you put before the people a law which does not make sense, and I think I have alluded to that. When you put before the public a law which is intricately linked with other laws which, taken altogether, govern an area of activity, and taken together do not seem to make very much sense, then you begin to get into real trouble because you begin to become incredible as a law maker. The public do not take very long to decide that.
When I say what I am going to say now, I mean no personal slight to the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) who has a very difficult task on his hands and who is doing everything he can to deal with a very difficult situation. In view of the remarks made last night by hon. members during another debate, I certainly think that most of us wish him well and want to help him in this job. So, this is no criticism of the Solicitor General. The fact of the matter is that these collateral laws controlling bail reform, parole, tickets of leave and the whole question of
May 16, 1973

what is and what is not life imprisonment, are laws that do not enjoy the confidence of the public at this time. It is because of this that the illogicality of the bill before us becomes, in my view, even more alarming.

speechtext:
Through you, Mr. Speaker, I extend my appreciation to my colleagues in the House for allowing me to continue.
Because of the basic illogicality of this bill, I now have to ask myself what I am to do as a member here voting according to his conscience. I do not believe that voting according to your conscience means that you should wander into the House of Commons, ignore everything you have seen, heard or been told by other people and suddenly apply some kind of star-struck wisdom from on high. I think what we do in this House when we vote according to our conscience depends to a great degree on how much attention we pay to what we hear outside this House. In many ridings the indication is that the majority of our citizens are in favour of retention of capital punishment. I am not certain what the feeling is in my own riding, although I have received 4,000 answers but I have not gone through them all. The feeling is probably very much along that line.
Capital Punishment
On the other hand, I probably have had the same experience as other members who have received letters in equal numbers from those who are for capital punishment and those who are against. Those letters have contained quotes from Scriptures and pleas to the effect that I vote according to my conscience. That is the dilemma most of us face.
I have for many years as a practicing lawyer advocated the complete abolition of capital punishment on the ground that, because our great system is made up of human beings and is by definition fallible, there is always the potential for error. There are other arguments for the abolition of capital punishment, but in my view at least that argument is completely irrefutable on any basis. We know that even if our Canadian judicial system has never made a mistake yet, it undoubtedly will because anything which is subject to human frailty will err sooner or later. So I would prefer that capital punishment be abolished entirely.
During the campaign I took the position when asked about this issue that I would prefer the abolition of capital punishment, but that I was not prepared to vote for an extension of the present system because I thought the law was basically illogical and other legislative areas were showing in practice to be deficient in protecting the security of the public. I recognize that in taking the position I do I may return to my riding pleasing no one. There must come a time I suppose in any member's parliamentary life when he must take that position whether he does it wittingly or unwittingly. Perhaps it is just as well that I am forced to take that position early in my parliamentary life.
I wish to close on this note. I would ask all hon. members to think carefully about how illogical this bill is, and to ask themselves why there is not something more logical presented to us. The government of the day has the power to place in front of Parliament a bill that would take these things into account. I must say it seems to me that in the early stages when this bill was being put together somebody from the government side did not adequately consider just what was being placed before the House. I do not think I have an obligation, no matter what my personal preference may be, to vote in favour of legislation which I believe to be fundamentally unsound and which does not appear to be logical, which draws distinctions which do not support morality but rather confound it.
